title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 24: Silahis v. Soluta: Liability of Private Persons Conducting Unreasonable Searches
keywords: Silahis International Hotel, Inc. v. Soluta
primary_topics: Chapter 24 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Silahis International Hotel, Inc. v. Soluta, in which the Court, through Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, held private persons civilly liable under Article 32 of the Civil Code for a warrantless search of a union office, once again upholding the inviolable right against unreasonable searches and seizures.

The core holding that the constitutional guarantee is not addressed to public officers alone: Article 32 makes any public officer, employee or private individual who violates the right to be secure against unreasonable searches liable in damages, including moral and, where warranted, exemplary damages.

The subsidiary rulings that defeated the hotel's defenses -- that ownership of the room did not deprive the union officers, as lawful occupants, of standing to question the search; that a waiver of the right cannot be presumed; and that liability extends to those indirectly responsible as well as to the actors.
sub_topics: The search arose in the employees' union office in the basement of Silahis Hotel, which management said it entered after reports of the sale or use of marijuana, dollar smuggling, prostitution and a theft syndicate, and after surveillance and the permission of union officer Henry Babay.

Respondents gave a different account: on the morning of January 11, 1988 union officer Soluta could not open the office door, a laundrywoman said she had seen five men in barong tagalog forcing it open at dawn, and when a locksmith was fetched, men in barong tagalog armed with clubs arrived and began hitting the employees.

While police were awaited, Petitioner Panlilio told Babay they would go to the union office to settle the mauling incident, ordered a security guard to force the door open, and searched over Babay's objection and his demand for a search warrant; a plastic bag of marijuana flowering tops was found and thirteen union officers were charged under the Dangerous Drugs Act.

The trial court acquitted the accused, holding that with the specimen inadmissible and the confiscation suspicious there was insufficient evidence; the union officers then sued for malicious prosecution and violation of their right against illegal search, and the trial court and the Court of Appeals held the hotel officers liable in damages.
Before the Supreme Court the petitioners argued mainly that the constitutional protection against illegal searches and seizures was not meant to be invoked against private individuals.

The Third Division denied the Petition, reiterating that such constitutional rights occupy a lofty position in every civilized and democratic community and that their violation, whether a penal offense or not, must be guarded against.

Article 32 of the Civil Code was quoted, making any public officer, employee or private individual who directly or indirectly impairs the enumerated rights -- including the right against unreasonable searches and seizures -- liable for damages, with indemnity to include moral damages and exemplary damages available as well.

The petitioners had admitted receiving reports of illegal activity in late 1987 and surveilling the office, yet barged in without a warrant despite ample time to obtain one, a course the Court said stinks in illegality for falling under none of the exceptional instances allowing a warrantless search.
The claim that the search was reasonable because the hotel owned the room was rejected: the respondents, as lawful occupants, still had the right to question the validity of the search and seizure.

The claim that Babay had consented was also rejected, a waiver requiring clear and convincing evidence that the right exists, that the person had actual or constructive knowledge of it, and that he actually intended to relinquish it, voluntarily and knowingly.

Because Article 32 reaches persons directly or indirectly responsible, the petitioners together with the security personnel who had orchestrated the illegal search were held jointly and severally liable for actual, moral and exemplary damages.

stances.claim: The constitutional protection against unreasonable searches and seizures may be invoked against private individuals, because lawmakers have deemed it necessary under Article 32 of the Civil Code to hold not only public officers but also private persons civilly liable for violating these rights.
stances.rhetorical_move: answering the petitioners' single main argument by quoting the statutory text that already resolves it

stances.claim: Having admitted that they had received reports and conducted surveillance since late 1987, the petitioners had ample time to obtain a warrant, so barging into the union office without one stinks in illegality, falling under none of the exceptional instances when a warrantless search is allowed.
stances.rhetorical_move: turning the petitioners' own admission of prior surveillance into proof that the exception could not apply

stances.claim: Neither ownership of the room nor a supposed consent saved the search: lawful occupants may question its validity, and a waiver of the right cannot be presumed but requires clear and convincing evidence of knowledge and of an actual, voluntary and intelligent intention to relinquish it.
stances.rhetorical_move: elimination of defenses in sequence, each met with a settled requisite

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 24 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Silahis International Hotel, Inc. v. Soluta et al., in which the Court, through Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, once again upheld the inviolable right of persons against warrantless and unreasonable searches and seizures -- this time against private persons. Hotel management said it had searched the employees' union office in the basement after reports of marijuana, dollar smuggling, prostitution and a theft syndicate, following surveillance and with the permission of union officer Henry Babay. The union's account differed: on the morning of January 11, 1988 officer Soluta found the office door jammed, a laundrywoman reported having seen five men in barong tagalog forcing it open at dawn, and when a locksmith was fetched, club-wielding men in barong tagalog arrived and beat the employees. While police were awaited, Petitioner Panlilio ordered a security guard to force the door, searched over Babay's objection and his demand for a warrant, and found marijuana flowering tops, on which thirteen union officers were charged under the Dangerous Drugs Act. The trial court acquitted them, finding the specimen inadmissible and the confiscation suspicious, and the officers then sued for malicious prosecution and violation of their right against illegal search, winning damages in the trial court and the Court of Appeals. Before the Supreme Court the petitioners argued chiefly that the constitutional guarantee could not be invoked against private individuals. The Third Division denied the Petition, holding that such rights occupy a lofty position in every civilized and democratic community and that Article 32 of the Civil Code makes any public officer, employee or private individual who directly or indirectly impairs them liable for damages. Since the petitioners had surveilled the office since late 1987 and had ample time to secure a warrant, their course stank in illegality; ownership of the room did not deprive the lawful occupants of standing to object; consent could not be presumed absent clear and convincing proof of a knowing and voluntary waiver; and because the article reaches those indirectly responsible, the petitioners and the security personnel who orchestrated the search were held jointly and severally liable for actual, moral and exemplary damages.
